title: Primary Function of the Selector Pin
learningObjectives: Identify the selector pin's mechanical function.
student: What is the mechanical purpose of the selector pin in a selectorized weight-stack machine?
instructor: The pin connects the cable-driven selector stem to the chosen weight plate so the stem can lift that plate and all plates above it.

title: External Load
learningObjectives: Relate the selected stack setting to connector load.
student: During the controlled constant-speed lift, what load must the selector pin transmit?
instructor: The pin transmits the force needed to support the selected moving stack. With negligible acceleration, vertical equilibrium gives P = mg = {{selector_load_N}} N.

title: Components Loading and Supporting the Pin
learningObjectives: Identify the local pin-loading components.
student: Identify the selector stem, selector pin, and selected plate. Which component loads the middle of the pin, and which material supports it?
instructor: The central selector stem loads the middle portion of the horizontal pin. Material from the selected plate supports the pin on the two sides of the stem.

title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace force transfer through the machine.
student: Trace the load path from the user to the selected weight-stack plates.
instructor: User → exercise bar → cable and pulleys → selector stem → selector pin → selected plate → plates stacked above it.

title: Critical Connection
learningObjectives: Explain why the pin is mechanically important.
student: Why is the selector pin a mechanically important connection in this load path?
instructor: The pin is the removable connector that transfers the entire selected-stack load from the stem into the plate. Loss of its load-transfer capacity would disconnect the selected stack from the lifting system.

title: Double-Shear Failure Mode
learningObjectives: Relate the connection geometry to two shear planes.
student: What connector failure mode is evaluated, and why is a double-shear model appropriate?
instructor: The assigned mode is average direct shear through the pin. The central stem load is resisted by selected-plate contact on both sides, creating two pin cross sections at which relative sliding could occur.
commonMistakes: Do not treat the two supporting sides as two separate pins; one pin has two resisting shear planes.

title: Controlling Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify the data required for the pin check.
student: Identify the assigned loading, geometry, material, and design parameters that control the pin shear stress and factor of safety.
instructor: The required data are Ws = {{selector_W_lb}} {{selector_W_lb_unit}}, d = {{selector_d_mm}} {{selector_d_mm_unit}}, Sy = {{selector_S_y_MPa}} {{selector_S_y_MPa_unit}}, FSreq = {{selector_FS_req}}, g = {{selector_g}} {{selector_g_unit}}, and two symmetric shear planes.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Develop a double-shear pin idealization from a physical connection.
student: Create a simplified connection model and free-body diagram of the selector pin. Show the central selector stem, selected-plate material on both sides, the horizontal pin, two shear planes, total load P, and equal reactions P/2.
instructor: A correct model shows the stem applying P to the middle of the pin, the selected plate providing two symmetric P/2 reactions, and shear planes at the two stem/plate interfaces. Label the circular pin diameter d and A = πd2/4.
gradingNotes: Students should construct this idealization before viewing the instructor reference image.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting the double-shear model.
student: State and justify the assumptions used to reduce the real machine to the assigned selector-pin model.
instructor: Treat the selected plates as one translating mass, use controlled constant speed so acceleration is negligible, assume symmetric direct shear and equal load sharing, use a circular smooth shank and uniform average stress, and neglect the excluded effects stated in the problem scope.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan a complete double-shear safety calculation.
student: Before substituting values, outline the calculations needed to evaluate and size the selector pin.
instructor: Convert the stack setting to mass; use P = mg; divide P equally between two shear planes; compute pin area and average shear stress; estimate shear yield and allowable stress; calculate actual factor of safety and minimum diameter; then make a bounded engineering assessment.

title: Selected Moving Mass
learningObjectives: Convert pound-mass to kilograms.
student: Convert the selected {{selector_W_lb}} {{selector_W_lb_unit}} stack setting to mass in kilograms using 1 lb = 0.45359237 kg.
instructor: m = ({{selector_W_lb}} lb)(0.45359237 kg/lb) = {{selector_mass_kg}} kg.

title: Constant-Speed Connector Load
learningObjectives: Apply vertical equilibrium at constant speed.
student: For controlled constant-speed lifting, determine the force P transmitted by the selector stem to the pin.
instructor: Because a ≈ 0, ΣFy = 0 gives P = mg = ({{selector_mass_kg}} kg)({{selector_g}} m/s2) = {{selector_load_N}} N.

title: Double-Shear Load Sharing
learningObjectives: Determine force on each shear plane.
student: Assuming symmetric load sharing, determine the shear force carried on each of the two shear planes.
instructor: Vplane = P/2 = {{selector_load_N}} N/2 = {{selector_force_per_plane_N}} N.

title: Pin Cross-Sectional Area
learningObjectives: Compute circular pin area.
student: For the {{selector_d_mm}} {{selector_d_mm_unit}} circular pin, calculate the area of one shear plane.
instructor: A = πd2/4 = π({{selector_d_mm}} mm)2/4 = {{selector_area_mm2}} mm2.

title: Average Double-Shear Stress
learningObjectives: Calculate average pin shear stress.
student: Calculate the average shear stress in the selector pin.
instructor: τavg = (P/2)/A = {{selector_force_per_plane_N}} N/{{selector_area_mm2}} mm2 = {{selector_tau_actual_MPa}} MPa.

title: Shear-Yield and Allowable Stress
learningObjectives: Estimate shear yield and allowable stress.
student: Using the tensile yield strength and von Mises criterion, estimate the pin's shear-yield strength and allowable shear stress.
instructor: τy = Sy/√3 = {{selector_S_y_MPa}} MPa/√3 = {{selector_tau_y_MPa}} MPa. Then τallow = τy/FSreq = {{selector_tau_allow_MPa}} MPa.

title: Actual Factor of Safety
learningObjectives: Calculate and interpret factor of safety.
student: Determine the actual factor of safety against estimated shear yielding and compare it with the requirement.
instructor: FSactual = τy/τavg = {{selector_tau_y_MPa}}/{{selector_tau_actual_MPa}} = {{selector_fos_actual}}. {{selector_fos_assessment}}

title: Minimum Required Pin Diameter
learningObjectives: Size a circular pin for double shear.
student: Determine the minimum smooth-shank pin diameter required to satisfy the specified factor of safety under the same load.
instructor: Set P/(2A) = τallow with A = πd2/4. Thus dmin = √[2P/(πτallow)] = {{selector_d_min_mm}} mm. {{selector_diameter_assessment}}

title: Sensitivity and Operating Condition
learningObjectives: Explain how load and acceleration affect pin stress.
student: Explain how increasing the selected stack mass changes pin shear stress. How would rapid upward acceleration affect pin load relative to the constant-speed case?
instructor: For fixed diameter, average shear stress increases linearly with selected mass. During upward acceleration, P = m(g + a), so the pin load and stress exceed the constant-speed values.

title: Engineering Assessment and Limitations
learningObjectives: Make a bounded selector-pin recommendation.
student: State whether the specified pin is adequate for the idealized load case and identify at least two effects that require consideration in a detailed product design.
instructor: {{selector_engineering_assessment}} A complete design must also check effects such as pin bending, plate and stem bearing, tear-out, fatigue, wear, clearance and impact, stress concentrations, material condition, and actual geometry.
gradingNotes: Do not award full credit for an unqualified statement that the complete machine is safe.
